topic: Day 1 · Approach to the Bleeding Patient — Resuscitate First
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Emergency & Acute Medical Unit
speakerBio: A resuscitationist who has run more GI-bleed calls than she can count and teaches that the endoscope never saved a patient who exsanguinated in the corridor. Her mantra: read the heart rate, not the blood pressure.
lectureHTML:
🎯 Where we start — 03:14, resus bay 2

A 47-year-old man is wheeled in vomiting bright red blood into a cardboard bowl. He is grey, sweating, and answers you slowly. Heart rate 122, BP 96/64, cap refill 4 seconds, and he has the caput medusae and spider naevi of a cirrhotic. The nurse is asking you what fluids to prescribe. Stop. Before you name a single drug, understand this: the patient in front of you is not dying of a diagnosis — he is dying of a volume of blood that has left his circulation. Everything this week hangs off one instinct: resuscitate first, diagnose second.

1 · The one sentence that holds the whole topic

In the actively bleeding patient, the first hour belongs to the circulation, not the endoscope. You resuscitate the patient you have before you localise the lesion you cannot yet see.

Gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding kills through a single final common pathway — haemorrhagic shock: the loss of enough intravascular volume that oxygen delivery to tissues collapses. The endoscopist who fixes the vessel is important, but they are downstream of the person who keeps the patient alive long enough to reach the scope. This session builds the mental model that governs the next three: resuscitate → risk-stratify → localise → treat. Get the order wrong and you can lose a patient with an entirely treatable lesion.

2 · The language of GI bleeding — say exactly what you see 🩸

The words are not interchangeable. Each one localises the bleed and predicts its danger. Learn them cold, because the vocabulary is the first diagnostic test.

TermWhat it isWhat it tells you
HaematemesisVomiting fresh red bloodBrisk upper GI bleed (proximal to the ligament of Treitz). Red = recent, fast, not yet acid-altered.
Coffee-ground vomitingVomiting dark, granular altered bloodUpper GI bleed that has been oxidised by gastric acid (haemoglobin → haematin). Slower or stopped bleeding — but never dismiss it; the pump may just be off for now.
MelaenaBlack, tarry, offensive-smelling, sticky stoolBlood that has spent time being digested — almost always upper GI (or slow right-colonic). It takes as little as ~50 mL of upper GI blood and several hours of transit to turn stool black.
HaematocheziaFresh red/maroon blood per rectumUsually a lower GI bleed — BUT a brisk upper bleed can transit so fast it comes out red. Red PR blood in a shocked patient is upper GI until proven otherwise.
💡 The melaena-vs-haematochezia clue to level

Colour is a clock, not just a location. Black means the blood was in the gut long enough to be digested → high and/or slow. Red means it came out fast → either low, or high-and-torrential. So melaena = upper GI, high probability; haematochezia = lower GI usually, but haematochezia + shock + a raised urea = a massive upper GI bleed screaming past you. Never let a red PR bleed talk you out of an upper source in a collapsing patient.

🎯 The urea clue

A raised urea with a normal creatinine in a bleeding patient is a fingerprint of an upper GI source: blood is a protein meal digested and absorbed in the small bowel (the "GI protein load"), spiking urea, while hypovolaemia adds a pre-renal component. A urea:creatinine ratio that is disproportionately high points the finger upstream even before endoscopy.

3 · Why blood loss kills — the physiology of haemorrhagic shock ⚙️

Shock is not "low blood pressure." Shock is inadequate tissue oxygen delivery. Blood pressure is one of the last things to fail, because the young cardiovascular system is superbly built to defend it. To resuscitate well you must understand exactly what the body is doing to compensate — and why that compensation is a trap.

Follow the vicious cycle step by step:

  1. Volume leaves the circulation. The vascular tank empties from the inside. Preload (venous return) falls.
  2. Stroke volume falls. Less preload → by the Frank–Starling relationship, each beat ejects less blood.
  3. The baroreceptors fire. Falling pressure triggers a massive sympathetic surge: tachycardia (to defend cardiac output) and vasoconstriction (to defend blood pressure and shunt blood to brain and heart).
  4. Blood pressure is held artificially normal. Systemic vascular resistance rises to compensate — so the number on the monitor lies. The patient is profoundly volume-deplete with a "normal" BP.
  5. The periphery is sacrificed. Skin and gut are clamped down: cold peripheries, prolonged capillary refill, oliguria, then rising lactate as starved tissues switch to anaerobic metabolism.
  6. Decompensation. When ~30–40% of blood volume is lost, vasoconstriction can no longer hold the pressure. BP falls off a cliff. This is not a gentle slope — it is a trapdoor.
A normal blood pressure in a bleeding young adult is not reassurance — it is the sound of a compensatory mechanism working at its limit, moments before it breaks.

The four classes of haemorrhagic shock (ATLS)

FeatureClass IClass IIClass IIIClass IV
Blood loss<15% (<750 mL)15–30% (750–1500 mL)30–40% (1500–2000 mL)>40% (>2000 mL)
Heart rate<100100–120120–140>140 (or brady, pre-arrest)
Blood pressureNormalNormal (narrowed pulse pressure)FallingMarkedly low
Pulse pressureNormalNarrowed (rising diastolic)NarrowedNarrowed
Mental stateSlightly anxiousMildly anxiousAnxious, confusedConfused, lethargic
Urine output>30 mL/h20–30 mL/h5–15 mL/hNegligible

Read that table across, not down. The single most dangerous cell is "Class II — blood pressure normal." A patient can have lost a third of their circulating volume with a systolic of 120. The tachycardia and narrowed pulse pressure (rising diastolic from vasoconstriction) are the early tells — long before the systolic drops.

⚠️ Danger — compensated shock in the young

Fit young adults, athletes, and pregnant patients compensate so well that they can look almost normal until they are nearly exsanguinated — then crash without warning. Beta-blockers (common in cirrhotics on non-selective beta-blockade for varices!) blunt the tachycardia, removing your earliest alarm. Never risk-stratify on blood pressure alone. Trend the heart rate, the pulse pressure, the lactate, the mental state, and the peripheries. A "normal" BP is the most reassuring-looking, most treacherous sign in the resus bay.

4 · The resuscitation — ABCDE for the bleeding patient 🚑

Bleeding is a "C problem," but you do not skip to it. You run the primary survey in order because the airway can kill this patient faster than the bleed.

A — Airway (and the variceal trap)

The patient who is vomiting large volumes of blood is at high risk of aspiration — blood in the lungs is both a chemical pneumonitis and a mechanical asphyxiant. A patient with a reduced conscious level (from shock, from hepatic encephalopathy, from the exhaustion of continuous vomiting) cannot protect their airway.

⚠️ Danger — the airway is the silent killer in variceal haematemesis

The classic avoidable death in massive upper GI bleeding is not exsanguination — it is aspiration of blood in an obtunded encephalopathic cirrhotic. If the patient is torrentially haematemesing, encephalopathic, or has a falling GCS, call for anaesthetics early and intubate to protect the airway before endoscopy. A controlled intubation in resus beats an emergency one over a lung full of blood on the endoscopy trolley. Do not wait for a "definite" indication — anticipate it.

B — Breathing

High-flow oxygen. Anaemic, hypoperfused tissues need every advantage in oxygen content and delivery. Watch for aspiration (new crackles, desaturation).

C — Circulation — the heart of resuscitation ❤️

  • Two large-bore cannulae. Insert two wide-bore (14G or 16G) peripheral IV lines, ideally in the antecubital fossae. This is non-negotiable and comes before almost everything else.
  • Why large and peripheral, not a central line? Flow through a tube obeys Poiseuille's law: flow ∝ radius⁴ / length. A short, fat peripheral cannula delivers blood far faster than a long, narrow central line. You can transfuse a shocked patient through two 14G peripheral lines faster than through most central catheters. Radius to the fourth power is the most important equation in resuscitation.
  • Bloods on cannulation: FBC (baseline Hb — but remember it lags acute loss), urea & electrolytes, LFTs, clotting/fibrinogen, and — critically — group & save + crossmatch. Activate the major haemorrhage protocol early if the patient is unstable (Session 2).
  • Fluids and blood: resuscitate to perfusion, not to a normal Hb. The transfusion strategy — restrictive, targeting Hb 70 — is the subject of Session 2, and it is one of the most counterintuitive and important lessons of the week.
💡 Pearl — the Hb that lies early

In acute haemorrhage the initial haemoglobin is normal — you lose whole blood, so the concentration is unchanged until fluid shifts and resuscitation fluids dilute it over hours. A "reassuring" Hb of 130 in a patient actively vomiting blood tells you almost nothing about how much they have lost. Resuscitate the patient, not the number.

D — Disability

Assess GCS. Falling consciousness may mean profound shock (cerebral hypoperfusion) or, in a cirrhotic, hepatic encephalopathy precipitated by the blood load — both are airway threats. Check glucose.

E — Exposure

Look for the stigmata of chronic liver disease (jaundice, ascites, spider naevi, caput medusae, palmar erythema) — they change your whole pathway toward the variceal bundle (Session 4). Do a rectal examination: confirm melaena or haematochezia. Keep the patient warm — hypothermia worsens coagulopathy.

5 · The first fork in the road — upper vs lower 🍴

Once resuscitation is underway, the single most useful early decision is: is this upper or lower? It determines who you call, which scope, and which drugs.

CluePoints UPPERPoints LOWER
PresentationHaematemesis, coffee-grounds, melaenaHaematochezia, fresh blood PR
Urea:creatinineDisproportionately raised ureaNormal ratio
Risk factorsNSAIDs, alcohol/cirrhosis, prior ulcer, H. pylori, retching (Mallory–Weiss)Diverticular disease, angiodysplasia, age, colorectal malignancy, recent polypectomy
HaemodynamicsMore often unstable / briskOften self-limiting (but can be massive)

Roughly 80% of GI bleeds are upper and most stop spontaneously — but the ones that don't are the ones that kill, and variceal bleeds carry the highest mortality. The instinct that saves lives: in the shocked patient, assume and treat for an upper GI bleed first, because it is both more likely and more lethal, and because a brisk upper bleed can masquerade as haematochezia.

⚠️ Danger — the "lower GI bleed" that was upper

Do not anchor. Maroon or even red PR blood in a hypotensive, tachycardic patient with a raised urea is a massive upper GI bleed until an upper endoscopy says otherwise. Sending such a patient for a colonoscopy prep instead of an urgent OGD wastes the golden hour on the wrong end of the gut.

6 · The mental model — the four verbs, in order 🧠

Everything in the management of GI bleeding fits into four sequential verbs. Say them like a mantra:

  1. Resuscitate — ABCDE, two large-bore cannulae, restore perfusion, protect the airway. (This session.)
  2. Risk-stratify — Glasgow-Blatchford, Rockall, AIMS65: who goes home, who needs an urgent scope. (Session 3.)
  3. Localise — history, examination, urea, and ultimately endoscopy, the definitive diagnostic and therapeutic tool.
  4. Treat — pharmacology to buy time (PPIs, prokinetics, the variceal bundle; Session 4), then definitive endoscopic, radiological (embolisation), or surgical haemostasis.
Resuscitate → risk-stratify → localise → treat. If you ever feel lost at the bedside of a bleeding patient, ask which verb you are on — and whether you skipped one.
☠️ M&M — "His pressure was fine"

A 31-year-old marathon runner presented with two episodes of coffee-ground vomiting and one small fresh haematemesis after a weekend of ibuprofen for a knee injury. Triage HR was 104, BP 124/86 — logged as "haemodynamically stable, for routine morning endoscopy." He was placed on a corridor trolley with a single 20G cannula and maintenance fluids. Over three hours his heart rate crept to 130 and his diastolic rose, but the systolic held at 118, so the alarm was never called. He then had one large haematemesis, vomited, aspirated, and arrested. Post-hoc, his estimated blood loss was Class III before he ever left triage — the tachycardia and narrowing pulse pressure in a fit young man were compensated shock, and the single narrow cannula could never have kept up with resuscitation. Lessons: (1) In the young, a normal systolic BP is the last thing to fail — read the heart rate and pulse pressure. (2) Two large-bore cannulae are placed in anticipation, not after the crash. (3) Continuous vomiting of blood is an airway emergency waiting to happen. He died of physiology that was fully visible three hours before his arrest.

7 · Take-home 🎯

  • Resuscitate first, diagnose second. The first hour belongs to the circulation, not the endoscope.
  • Name what you see: haematemesis/coffee-grounds = upper; melaena = upper (digested = high/slow); haematochezia = lower usually, but upper-and-torrential in the shocked patient.
  • Shock is inadequate oxygen delivery — blood pressure fails last. A normal BP in the young is compensated shock, not safety.
  • Learn the four ATLS classes; the danger cell is Class II with a "normal" BP and narrowed pulse pressure.
  • ABCDE: protect the airway (variceal aspiration kills), two 14–16G cannulae (Poiseuille: flow ∝ radius⁴), crossmatch, activate major haemorrhage if unstable.
  • The early Hb lies — resuscitate the patient, not the number.
  • Hold the model: resuscitate → risk-stratify → localise → treat.

Next session: the single most important — and most counterintuitive — decision in resuscitation of the GI bleed. When you finally give blood, how much is too much? Villanueva, the restrictive strategy, and the harm of over-transfusion.

moderatorQs.q: A 25-year-old presents with haematemesis. His blood pressure is 118/84 and heart rate 108. The triage nurse calls him 'stable.' Why should that word worry you?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because in a fit young adult a normal systolic blood pressure is the last thing to fail, not a marker of safety. His sympathetic nervous system is defending that pressure with intense vasoconstriction and tachycardia — the tachycardia (108) and, crucially, any narrowing of the pulse pressure (rising diastolic from vasoconstriction) are the early signatures of compensated Class II shock, in which up to 30% of blood volume can already be lost. When the young heart can no longer compensate, the pressure does not drift down gently — it falls off a trapdoor into decompensated shock. 'Stable' should be replaced by 'compensated, and therefore dangerous.' You trend heart rate, pulse pressure, lactate, mental state and peripheries, secure two large-bore cannulae, and prepare to transfuse — you do not relax.

moderatorQs.q: During resuscitation, why do we insist on two short wide-bore peripheral cannulae rather than reaching first for a central venous catheter?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: Because of Poiseuille's law: flow is proportional to the fourth power of the radius and inversely proportional to length. A short, fat peripheral cannula (14–16G in the antecubital fossa) permits far higher flow rates than a long, narrow central catheter — you can transfuse blood into a shocked patient dramatically faster peripherally. Doubling the radius increases flow sixteen-fold, whereas a longer line reduces it. In active haemorrhage the priority is rapid volume/blood replacement, so two large-bore peripheral lines are the correct first move; a central line is for pressors and monitoring, not for speed of resuscitation. Radius-to-the-fourth is the most important equation at the bedside of a bleeding patient.

moderatorQs.q: A cirrhotic patient with massive haematemesis has a GCS of 11 and is still vomiting blood. The endoscopy suite is ready. What is your priority, and why?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The priority is the airway, not the endoscope. The classic avoidable death in variceal haematemesis is not exsanguination but aspiration of blood in an obtunded, often encephalopathic patient who cannot protect their airway. With a falling GCS and ongoing torrential haematemesis you should call anaesthetics and perform a controlled endotracheal intubation to secure the airway before endoscopy. A planned intubation in resus is far safer than an emergency one over a lung full of blood on the endoscopy trolley, and a secured airway actually makes the endoscopy safer and more effective. Anticipate the indication rather than waiting for the crash.

audienceQs.q: A patient has fresh red blood per rectum but is shocked with a high urea. Everyone taught me haematochezia means a lower GI bleed — so why is the registrar calling for an upper endoscopy?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Because colour is a clock as much as a location. Haematochezia usually means a lower source, but a brisk upper GI bleed can transit the gut so fast that the blood emerges red rather than being digested to black melaena. Two features here override the rule of thumb: the patient is shocked (a marker of a large-volume, brisk bleed) and has a disproportionately raised urea (the digested-blood 'protein meal' plus pre-renal effect — a fingerprint of an upper source). Red blood PR in a hypotensive, tachycardic patient with a high urea is a massive upper GI bleed until an OGD proves otherwise. Sending them for a colonoscopy prep would waste the golden hour on the wrong end of the gut.

audienceQs.q: The patient is clearly bleeding a lot, but his first haemoglobin came back at 132. Doesn't that mean he hasn't lost much?
audienceQs.answerHTML: No — the early haemoglobin is one of the great traps. In acute haemorrhage you lose whole blood: red cells and plasma leave together, so the concentration (which is what Hb measures) stays normal at first. The Hb only falls hours later as fluid shifts from the interstitium and as your resuscitation fluids dilute the remaining blood. So a 'reassuring' Hb of 132 in someone actively vomiting blood reflects how recently they bled, not how little. Resuscitate the patient in front of you — heart rate, pulse pressure, perfusion, lactate — not the number on the gas. Send a crossmatch and repeat the Hb, but never let an early normal value delay resuscitation.

audienceQs.q: When you say 'resuscitate first,' where does the diagnosis actually fit in? It feels wrong to treat before we know the cause.
audienceQs.answerHTML: It feels wrong but it is exactly right, and there is a fixed order that makes it safe: resuscitate → risk-stratify → localise → treat. The patient in shock is dying from the volume of blood lost, not from the specific lesion, and the compensatory mechanisms buy only minutes. So we run ABCDE, place two large-bore cannulae, send a crossmatch, protect the airway and restore perfusion before we know whether it is an ulcer or a varix — because those interventions are identical regardless of the cause and cannot wait. The diagnosis (localise) comes at endoscopy, once the patient is stable enough to reach it alive. If you ever feel lost, ask which of the four verbs you are on — and whether one was skipped.
